newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Reform ghosts haunt Russia's new fix-it team.
newsitem.headline: Reform ghosts haunt Russia's new fix-it team.

text.p: Russia's reformers brought in to fix the anaemic economy are haunted by the experience of an earlier young group which five years ago offered a bold new programme but saw it wither away.

In late 1991 President Boris Yeltsin, riding a huge wave of popularity and running a newly-independent country on the brink of economic collapse, brought in a young team of little-known reformers and academics, headed by Yegor Gaidar and Anatoly Chubais, to carry out dramatic changes.
They filled the shop shelves in months but also unleashed inflation which made millions poor.

In December 1992, Yeltsin bowed to pressure from the conservative parliament and replaced Gaidar with industrial boss Viktor Chernomyrdin, who called Gaidar's team of academics "heads of laboratories", ill-qualified to run the huge state.
By January 1996, Chubais was the only member of the Gaidar team left in the cabinet and Yeltsin sacked him as well.

This week, Yeltsin, recovered from eight months of illness and facing stagnating reforms, reshuffled the cabinet in a way similar to 1991 and set up a new team in which Chubais plays a key role and Gaidar acts behind the scene as his guru.
They face a tremendous task and the sad experience of the first effort of "shock therapy" must be vivid in their memories.
"People in charge in 1991 had not had experience making things happen," said Per Maelstrom, head of research at Moscow's Brunswick brokerage.
"Chubais is an administrator. He knows what the stumbling blocks are and he should be better at avoiding them.
"Things will have to change," Maelstrom said. "If (Chubais's team) has not at least given reason to be optimistic in six months, people will start to attack."
He said Chernomyrdin would support reformers but conservatives in the government and parliament would not hold off more than half a year unless Russians supported reform.
"There will not be an improvement in living standards in six months, but you might have pensions paid in time -- you will get your pay, but you have to pay more for your housing," he said.
Jim Nail, head of research at Deutche Morgan Grenfell, said Yeltsin would give reformers three years, until the next parliamentary elections, to improve living standards.
"The (recent) shuffle, especially the economics-oriented portfolios, shows that Chubais has been given a mandate by the president to radicalise economic reform," Nail said.
Chubais, now 41, is joined as first deputy prime minister by land reform pioneer and governor of Nizhny Novgorod region Boris Nemtsov, 37, and some conservatives.
The group is not much older than Gaidar and his colleagues were but it has an impressive amount of experience.

Vladimir Konovalov, chief economist at the World Bank in Moscow, said Gaidar's academics, used to running classrooms, were faced with the largest combined political and economic reform in history and a population wary of capitalism.
"That Gaidar was able to open up Russia without it completely falling apart was a remarkable achievement," he said.
"The key now is to get structural reforms in place and put Russia on a sustainable growth path."

Economists said the government would have to make an extremely unpopular move of cutting state support of housing, which Nail said accounted for four percent of gross domestic product, and other communal services.
Russia desparately needs to improve tax collection and reform its tax code and has said it will reform natural monopolies.
Nail said Chubais would probably move quickly to get the worst over for average Russians.
"I think there was a bit of a popular reform mandate in 1992 and I think a lot of that has probably been used up."
